title: Fractions: Add & Subtract
subtitle: You cannot add pieces until they are the same size.
objectives: Explain why fractions need a common denominator
Find the lowest common denominator of two fractions
Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators
Convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions
Add and subtract mixed numbers, including regrouping
Simplify a fraction to lowest terms

cards.title: Half plus a third is not two fifths
cards.text: That is the most common wrong answer in this whole topic, and it comes from adding the bottoms. The bottoms are not amounts.

cards.title: The bottom names the piece. The top counts them
cards.text: In 3/4, the 4 says the whole was cut into four. The 3 says you have three of those.
points: **Denominator** — how many pieces the whole was cut into.
**Numerator** — how many of those you have.
**The bottom is a name**, not a quantity.
**You never add names.** You add counts.

cards.title: Why the bottoms have to match
cards.text: Tap through the three steps. This is the whole method in pictures.

question.text: Why can you not add 1/2 and 1/3 directly?
options: One is bigger than the other
You can, and the answer is 2/5
question.explain: Different sized pieces cannot be counted together. Re-cut both into sixths first.

cards.title: Find the lowest common denominator
cards.text: The smallest number that both denominators divide into. Then change both fractions to use it.
points: **Whatever you do to the bottom, do to the top.**
**1/2 becomes 3/6** because you multiplied both by 3.
**The value has not changed.** Only the name.

question.text: What is 1/4 + 1/2? Give your answer as a fraction.
question.explain: Change 1/2 to 2/4. Then 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. The bottom stays 4.

cards.title: You cannot add millimetres to inches
cards.text: A spanner set in inches and a bolt in millimetres are the same problem. Convert to one unit first, then the numbers mean something.
points: **Different units cannot be added.**
**A denominator is a unit.**
**Convert first, then add.** Same rule.
**Mechanics own two sets of spanners** for exactly this.

cards.title: A fraction is meaningless without the whole
cards.text: A quarter of a stack sounds like one number. In Minecraft it depends entirely on what the item is.
points: **Most items stack to 64.** A quarter is 16.
**Ender pearls stack to 16.** A quarter is 4.
**Same fraction, different amount.**
**The denominator is the whole.** That is why it matters.

cards.title: Always reduce at the end
cards.text: Divide the top and bottom by the same number until nothing divides them both. The value never changes.
points: **6/12 → divide both by 6 → 1/2.**
**Find the biggest number that divides both.**
**An answer left as 6/12 usually loses a mark.**
**Check it every time**, before you write the answer.

question.explain: Divide both by 4. 4/6 is not finished — both still divide by 2.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Simple fractions done. Part 2 is mixed numbers, which are the same thing carrying a whole. Your place is saved.

cards.title: A whole and a bit, written two ways
cards.text: Two and a half is 2½, or it is 5/2. Same amount. Which one you use depends on what you are about to do with it.

cards.title: Mixed to improper, and back
cards.text: Two conversions, each one a single sentence. Learn them as a procedure, not as an idea.
points: **Mixed → improper:** whole × bottom, + top, keep the bottom.
**Improper → mixed:** divide, the remainder is the top.

cards.title: Two safe routes, and one is safer
cards.text: You can add the wholes and fractions separately, or convert everything to improper first. The second one never goes wrong.
points: **Separately** is faster when the fractions add to under one.
**Improper first** always works, including when they do not.
**Under pressure, convert.** Fewer decisions.
**Convert the answer back** at the end.

cards.title: Rounds and half rounds add up the same way
cards.text: Three and a half rounds plus two and three quarter rounds. You cannot add halves to quarters until they match.
points: **Change the half into two quarters.**
**5/4 is more than one**, so it becomes 6¼.
**That is regrouping**, in real timing.

cards.title: Subtracting when the top is too small
cards.text: 3¼ − 1¾. You cannot take three quarters from one quarter, so you borrow a whole and turn it into quarters.
points: **Borrow 1 from the 3**, leaving 2.
**That 1 becomes 4/4**, so ¼ becomes 5/4.
**Or convert both to improper** and avoid it entirely.

question.explain: 13/4 − 7/4 = 6/4 = 1½. Or borrow a whole and regroup, which gives the same answer.

terms.def: The top number. How many pieces you have.
The bottom number. How many pieces the whole was cut into.
A bottom number that both fractions can use.
The smallest number both denominators divide into.
A fraction whose top is bigger than its bottom, such as 5/2.
A whole number and a fraction together, such as 2½.
Divide top and bottom by the same number until nothing divides both.
Borrowing a whole and turning it into fractions, to subtract.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Never add the bottoms.** They are names, not amounts.
**Find the lowest common denominator first.**
**Convert mixed to improper** when it gets awkward.
**Simplify the answer**, every time.

quiz.text: Why do fractions need a common denominator before adding?
options: The pieces must be the same size to be counted together
So the answer is always simplified
quiz.explain: A denominator names the piece size. Different sizes cannot be counted together.
quiz.objective: Explain why fractions need a common denominator

quiz.text: What is the lowest common denominator of 1/4 and 1/6?
quiz.explain: 12 is the smallest number both 4 and 6 divide into. 24 works but is not the lowest.
quiz.objective: Find the lowest common denominator of two fractions

quiz.explain: False, and it is the classic error. You never add the bottoms. The answer is 5/6.

teacher.summary: Week 7 Math covers adding and subtracting fractions, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. It opens on the error it exists to prevent — adding the denominators — and answers it with a claim that fixes it permanently: the bottom number is a name for the piece size, not a quantity, and you never add names. The fractionBars figure carries that argument visually, because seeing two bars re-cut into sixths settles it faster than any explanation. The mixed-number half offers two methods and is explicit that converting to improper fractions is the one that never fails, which matters under exam pressure where the separate-wholes method breaks exactly when the fractions do not cooperate.
discussion: Ask him what 1/2 + 1/3 is before the lesson. If he says 2/5, this lesson is exactly what he needs.
Ask why the denominator is like a unit. Millimetres and inches make it obvious.
Ask him to explain regrouping in his own words. If it comes out as borrowing, he has it.
Ask which method he would use in an exam and why. Convert-to-improper is the defensible answer.
teacher.extension: Have him halve a recipe that uses ¾ cup and ⅔ cup of things. The arithmetic is unavoidable and the answer has to be usable with real measuring cups.
misconceptions: 'Add the tops and the bottoms.' The bottom names the piece size. Adding names is meaningless.
'The common denominator has to be the two multiplied together.' That always works but is often not the lowest.
'4/6 is a finished answer.' Both still divide by 2. Simplify until nothing divides both.
'You cannot subtract when the top is smaller.' Borrow a whole and turn it into fractions, or convert to improper first.
